When you’re “done” with this class…you’re not done.
You’ve just begun.
I want peers who can do what I can do, and ultimately exceed me
Mastery requires spending significant time outside of class honing your skills

Alright, before we start this class in earnest, I want to set the stage by way of my motivation for why I’m teaching this class. What it really comes down to is that I want peers who know what I know, can do what I can do, and can ultimately exceed me. I want more cool kids doing cool work that I can watch a presentation of and say “that’s cool!”

But I’ve obviously got a bit of a head start on you if you’re going to exceed me, yes? Which is why you need to understand that while I want to help get you to my level ASAP, that’s not going to happen if you just watch this class and then call it a day. Mastery of these skills will require spending significant time outside of class honing your skills. Like, hundreds to thousands of hours. Obviously that’s why your best option is to get a job which lets you get paid to keep honing your skills. That’s how I got my thousands of hours in after all.

So anyway, I just wanted you to know before you’re more than 1 slide into this class, that these videos are not the end, they’re just the beginning. I have high expectations of the students who start down our learning paths, and I hope that you’ll rise to meet them.
About the Class
The intent of this class is to expose you to the most commonly generated assembly instructions, and the most frequently dealt with architecture hardware.
64 bit instructions/hardware
Implementation of a Stack
Common debugging/disassembling tools
Many things will therefore be intentionally left out or deferred to later classes.
Floating point/vector instructions/hardware
16 bit instructions/hardware
Complicated or rare instructions
Instruction pipeline, alternate modes of operation, hardware virtualization, etc (see other classes for those)

Alright, so what are we going to learn in this class? The main thing is that I want you to learn above the most common assembly, registers, how the stack works, and what kind of tools you need in order to keep learning after class.

This means that I’m explicitly leaving out less common things like floating point instructions and registers, complicated and rare instructions, and many other things which will instead show up in more advanced classes.
About the Class 2
The hope is that the material covered will be provide the required background to delve deeper into areas which may have seemed daunting previously.

Because I can’t anticipate the needs of all job classes, if there are specific areas which you think would be useful to certain job types, let me know. The focus areas are currently primarily influenced by my security background, but I would like to make the class as widely applicable as possible.

Miss Alaineous
It’s called x86 because of the progression of Intel chips from 8086, 80186, 80286, etc.

Originally 16-bit architecture. Later evolved to 32 and 64-bit, but kept the backwards compatibility. The hardware actually starts up in 16 bit before software transitions it to 32 or 64 bit operation.
OK, a few quick miscellaneous points:
The name x86 comes from the fact that Intel’s first chip to use this instruction set had a model number of 8086. Then they came out with the 80186, 80286 and so forth.

The 8086 was a 16-bit architecture, which means it had 16-bit registers, a 16-bit memory space, etc. Later on when Intel expanded it to 32 bit and then later 64 bit, they always kept the backwards compatibility. So in reality when most hardware first powers on, it is actually running in 16 bit mode. Which we’ll talk about more in a future advanced architecture class.
Miss Alaineous 2

Intel originally wanted to break from x86 when moving to 64 bit. This was IA64 (Intel Architecture 64 bit) aka Itanium. However, AMD decided to extend x86 to 64 bits itself, leading to the AMD64 architecture. When Itanium had very slow adoption, Intel decided to bite the bullet and license the 64 bit extensions from AMD.
In the Intel manuals you will see the 64 bit extensions referred to as IA32e or EMT64 or Intel 64 (but never IA64. Again, that's Itanium, a completely different architecture).

Now when Intel originally was going to move from 32 bit to 64 bit, they were actually going to make a whole new architecture with all new instructions. This was known as Itanium, or IA64. But in parallel AMD decided to just extend 32 bit x86 to 64 bits in a fairly straightforward way. In the end Itanium didn’t really get widespread adoption, and Intel was forced to backpedal and license the 64 bit extensions from AMD.
In the Intel manuals this has a bunch of different names like IA32e, EMT64, and Intel 64.
Miss Alaineous 3
You might sometimes see it called amd64 or x64 by MS or some linux distributions
In this class we're going to go with x86-64
Other names you might seen in Linux distributions or from Microsoft are amd64 or x64. But in this class we’re going to call it x86-64.
Where is x86-64 used?
More powerful (but thus power-hungry) systems such as PCs, servers, and even super-computers

Minimal adoption on phones or embedded systems. Intel does have the entire Atom line of lower-power chips targeted towards embedded systems though (and they’re starting to focus more on performance per Watt, which is where ARM has always been better)

So where is x86-64 used? Well you probably know that it’s mostly used in applications which need high computational power, such as PCs, servers, and even super-computers. With very high probability, the machine you’re watching this class on is an x86-64 machine. But the ARM-based systems, like Microsoft Surface or Apple’s M1 Macs - which I helped design the SecureBoot system for - are coming to give Intel a run for it’s money in the PC space.
Intel has some chips which are more focused on power-constrained devices, like embedded systems, but they make up a tiny fraction of Intel’s chip volume.

But at the end of the day the simplest version remains this 6-instruction version, here shown disassembled by yet another disassembler, IDA. We can see the basic outline of what’s going on here. We see something referencing the string “Hello World”, we see a call to the printf() function. And we see the number hex 1234 which is what this version of Hello World returned at the end. The rest of the assembly, well we’ve got no idea yet what’s going on there.
Take Heart!
By one measure, only 14 assembly instructions account for 90% of code!
You’ve already seen 10 common instructions, just in the hello world variations! (And 2 special security instructions we’ll talk about later.)
I think that knowing about 20-30 (not counting variations) is good enough that you will have the check the manual very infrequently

But take heart! By one measure, only 14 assembly instructions account for 90% of code! And you’ve already seen 10 common instructions just in the different versions of Hello World that different compilers generate!
My personal experience is that if you know about 30 instructions, you will be able to read most code, and only need to hit up the manual very infrequently.

Outcomes
By the end of this class you should…
Know the x86-64 general purpose registers, and their 32 and 16 bit sub-register names
Understand how data like local variables or return addresses are stored on the stack
Understand function calling conventions
Be comfortable writing C code in an IDE (like Visual Studio) and reading and stepping through the disassembly (so you can find new instructions)
Be able to read assembly well enough to determine the expected inputs to influence the control flow for an opaque binary (the infamous “Binary Bomb lab”)
Alright, so what’s the final outcome going to be from this class?
By the end I expect that you should know all the x86-64 general purpose registers, and the older 32 and 16 bit register names, which can still be accessed by 64 bit code.
